      # CPLD build and simulation workspace
      
      This directory contains the headless Diamond build system and GHDL/cocotb
      simulator, sharing program manifests and one Sphinx documentation project.
      It is standalone: copy or rename this directory, install the documented tools,
      and run its Makefile without the old repository.
      
      ```sh
      cd new_approach  # from the repository root
      make list
      make build PROGRAM=tx30
      make sim
      make test-container
      make docs-container
      ```
      
      Start with the [shared quickstart](docs/getting-started.rst) and
      [environment setup](docs/environments.rst). See the [layout](docs/layout.rst),
      [build guide](docs/builds.rst), [simulation guide](docs/simulation.rst),
      [configuration](docs/configuration.rst), and [Python API](docs/api.rst).
      `make docs-container` creates `docs/_build/html/index.html`.
      
      - `buildsystem/`: Python CLI, validated model, workflow and Diamond backend.
      - `simulation/`: shared pytest/GHDL runner.
      - `programs/<name>/`: `<name>.toml`, `<name>.vhdl`,
        `<name>_constraints.lpf`, and `<name>_tb.py` (cocotb).
      - `targets/`: board configuration. Existing programs serve as cloning sources.
      - `toolchain_tests/`: build-tool self-tests and an optional licensed Diamond integration check.
      - `.devcontainer/`: unified Dockerfile, VS Code configuration and Diamond launchers.
      - `docs/`: unified current documentation; `docs/history/` holds earlier records.
      - `build/`: ignored firmware, reports, simulation traces and validation evidence.
      
      The repository root Makefile forwards the same commands. The three catalog programs use local VHDL and LPF copies. The originals are not used. Optional comparisons require an explicit external
      `--legacy-project` path. Building does not
      program hardware. GUI interaction and hardware release qualification remain
      separate acceptance steps.
      
      Create a program from any existing one with
      `make new NAME=my_adapter TEMPLATE=tx30`. This copies the current program files,
      renames them, and updates the manifest. There is no separate template directory.
      
      `make sim` uses the same image as CI and runs directly inside the Dev Container.
      No local virtual environment is used. Rebuild the Dev Container to install the
      unified build, simulation and documentation tools.

      # Diamond development container
      
      This environment runs the implemented headless program build frontend and its Sphinx documentation.
      It uses Ubuntu 22.04 and mounts an existing Linux x86-64 Diamond installation
      read-only. Neither Diamond binaries nor license files are copied into the image.
      The Docker build context is restricted to the environment files.
      
      ## Launch in VS Code
      
      Install Docker Engine on Linux and the VS Code **Dev Containers** extension.
      Start VS Code with the installation root in its environment (the directory
      above `bin`, not `bin/lin64`):
      
      ```sh
      export DIAMOND_HOST_ROOT="$HOME/lscc/diamond/3.14"
      code .
      ```
      
      Then select **Dev Containers: Reopen in Container**. If VS Code was already
      running without this variable, fully quit it and launch again from this shell.
      An empty `DIAMOND_HOST_ROOT` causes a bind-mount error. The Docker daemon must
      run on the machine containing that path and the checkout.
      
      After changing the Dockerfile or Dev Container configuration, use the Command
      Palette (`Ctrl+Shift+P`): **Dev Containers: Rebuild and Reopen in Container**
      from the host, or **Dev Containers: Rebuild Container** when already attached.
      Reopening an existing container alone does not apply Dockerfile changes.
      The bind-mounted repository is retained; manual installs and unmounted
      container-local files are replaced. See [VS Code rebuild instructions](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/devcontainers/create-dev-container#_rebuild).
      
      ## Codex and development utilities
      
      The image includes `curl`, `ripgrep`, and the standalone Codex CLI. VS Code
      also requests the `openai.chatgpt` Codex extension inside the development
      environment. After rebuilding, verify in a new container terminal:
      
      ```sh
      curl --version
      codex --version
      codex
      ```
      
      Sign in when prompted. Authentication is not baked into the image or copied
      from the host; container-local login/configuration may need restoring after a
      rebuild. The CLI is installed as `vscode` under its home directory using the
      [official Codex installer](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/codex/cli).
      The Docker build argument `CODEX_VERSION` defaults to `latest`; pass a release
      version to pin it. Cached layers do not automatically refresh `latest`; use a
      version change or a rebuild without cache when intentionally updating Codex.
      The [IDE extension](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/codex/ide) is installed by VS
      Code when attaching, independently of the command-line image build.
      
      For temporary additional apt packages, refresh metadata and use sudo:
      
      ```sh
      sudo apt-get update
      sudo apt-get install -y <package-name>
      ```
      
      The image removes apt lists to reduce its size, so package lookup may fail
      until `apt-get update` runs. Add lasting dependencies to the Dockerfile and
      rebuild instead of relying on manual installations.
      
      ## Diamond commands
      
      The container mounts Diamond at `/opt/diamond`. Inside it:
      
      ```sh
      check-diamond
      check-diamond --synthesis
      diamond-cli /path/to/script.tcl
      ```
      
      The first check runs automatically after container creation. It verifies Tcl
      project commands with DISPLAY and WAYLAND_DISPLAY unset. The optional second
      check synthesizes a temporary one-gate XO2 design using LSE, exercising the
      current licensing setup. It does not route, export firmware, or program hardware.
      Temporary smoke-test files are removed when the check exits.
      
      Configuration:
      
      | Variable | Location | Purpose |
      | --- | --- | --- |
      | `DIAMOND_HOST_ROOT` | Host environment before starting VS Code | Installation to mount |
      | `DIAMOND_ROOT` | Container environment, default `/opt/diamond` | Installation used by `diamond-cli` |
      | `LM_LICENSE_FILE` | Optional host environment, passed into container | Additional license file or `port@server` |
      
      Diamond's own `diamondc` wrapper configures Tcl/shared libraries and prepends
      `$DIAMOND_ROOT/license/license.dat` to the license search path. This existing
      license directory is included in the read-only installation mount. If using
      another license file, add a separate read-only mount and set `LM_LICENSE_FILE`
      to its **container** path. A host-only absolute license path will not work.
      
      ## Why mount Diamond and use host networking?
      
      Mounting reuses the installation already available on this machine. Installing
      inside the image would require the installer and installation automation, and
      would not remove the runtime license host-ID requirement.
      
      On native Linux, `--network=host` shares the host network namespace, so the
      container can see the host interfaces. This is the initial approach for reusing
      the existing node-locked license without setting a synthetic MAC. It also means
      the container shares host network access; it has no separate network namespace.
      See [Docker host networking](https://docs.docker.com/engine/network/drivers/host/).
      
      License success still depends on the existing license and FlexNet's interface
      detection. Lattice documents both MAC-based licensing and possible interface-name
      issues in its [license troubleshooting FAQ](https://www.latticesemi.com/en/Support/AnswerDatabase/4/7/4/4742).
      Do not change the host NIC MAC or edit the signed license. If this setup fails,
      compare the vendor `lmutil lmhostid` output on host and container locally, then
      use the appropriate license configuration or request rehosting. A dedicated
      container MAC is a possible later deployment design with a matching authorized
      license; it is not needed merely to install Diamond. Moving to another host
      will require revisiting licensing even if the image is identical.
      
      For a floating license, pass the license-server address through
      `LM_LICENSE_FILE`; host networking is not inherently required for that model.
      This setup targets native Linux, not Docker Desktop's VM network semantics.
      
      ## Build and run without VS Code
      
      From the repository root:
      
      ```sh
      export DIAMOND_HOST_ROOT="$HOME/lscc/diamond/3.14"
      docker build -t uz-cpld-diamond:3.14 .devcontainer
      docker run --rm --network=host \
        --mount "type=bind,source=$DIAMOND_HOST_ROOT,target=/opt/diamond,readonly" \
        uz-cpld-diamond:3.14 check-diamond --synthesis
      ```
      
      For an interactive development shell, also bind the repository and use `-it`:
      
      ```sh
      docker run --rm -it --network=host \
        --mount "type=bind,source=$DIAMOND_HOST_ROOT,target=/opt/diamond,readonly" \
        --mount "type=bind,source=$PWD,target=/workspaces/uz_cpld" \
        uz-cpld-diamond:3.14 bash
      ```
      
      The image user defaults to UID/GID 1000. VS Code adjusts it to the local user.
      For direct Docker use with a different UID/GID, build with `--build-arg
      USER_UID=... --build-arg USER_GID=...`.
      
      For rootless Podman, replace `docker` with `podman` and add
      `--userns=keep-id` to run commands so host installation/workspace permissions
      match. CLI validation here used Podman 3.4.2. Current
      [VS Code documentation](https://code.visualstudio.com/remote/advancedcontainers/docker-options)
      describes Podman 5+ compatibility. For a Podman Dev Container, set the local
      VS Code setting `dev.containers.dockerPath` to `podman` and add
      `--userns=keep-id` to `runArgs` in `devcontainer.json`. Docker does not accept
      that Podman-specific option. No Compose provider is required by this setup.
      
      ## Native GUI compatibility
      
      Continue launching the native host GUI with:
      
      ```sh
      "$DIAMOND_HOST_ROOT/bin/lin64/diamond" /host/path/to/project.ldf
      ```
      
      The container does not forward a display server or launch the GUI. Future
      generated projects use relative source paths and can be regenerated for
      the host, so paths such as `/workspaces/...` do not prevent native GUI use.
      Do not build the same project simultaneously from container and GUI.
      Useful GUI project/strategy changes are transferred manually into configuration.
      
      ## Reproducibility and next work
      
      Ubuntu 22.04 is listed in the installed Diamond 3.14 release notes. The image
      includes its distribution Python 3.10, `tomli`, Sphinx, and Tcl test support.
      The frontend uses a `tomllib`/`tomli` fallback. Ubuntu's image tag and apt packages are not
      digest/snapshot pinned yet. The mounted Diamond installation is external state;
      build provenance records the reported version and launcher hash. Pinning the image
      digest and package snapshot is later reproducibility work.
      
      The frontend now supports `tx30`, `rx30`, and `tx26_w_enable`, template creation,
      project generation, both firmware exports, and provenance. Run `make doctor`,
      `make build-all`, `make test`, and `make docs` from the repository root.
      See [the Sphinx documentation](../new_approach/docs/index.rst) for the full workflow
      and Python API. Rebuild the image to include the new Sphinx and test dependencies.
      Native GUI interaction and hardware acceptance remain manual checks.
      Netlist PDF/SVG export is deferred.
      
      See [the design and decision record](../cpld_toolchain.md) for the full plan and

      # CPLD toolchain plan
      
      Status: first build frontend implemented, 2026-09-16. The current user and Python
      API documentation is the [Sphinx project](new_approach/docs/index.rst)
      (`make docs`). The sections below retain the design decisions and historical
      repository observations; see the implementation session record at the end for
      current results and remaining acceptance checks.
      
      ## Scope and decisions
      
      | Topic | Decision or proposal | Status |
      | --- | --- | --- |
      | First hardware | UltraZohm Rev05+ D-slot MachXO2, `LCMXO2-2000HC-4TG100C` | Requested |
      | Workflow | Create programs and build files completely headlessly; retain Diamond GUI compatibility | Requested |
      | First backend | Diamond first; add the open-source backend after a reference build works. Use LSE as the proposed synthesis engine. | Backend order confirmed by user; LSE carried from existing projects |
      | Frontend | Thin Makefile over a Python CLI, TOML manifests, Diamond Tcl backend | Proposed |
      | Program creation | Generate editable VHDL and a manifest from a named template; users then edit VHDL | Confirmed by user |
      | First hosts | Linux headless builds in a development container and native Linux Diamond GUI | Confirmed by user; container setup precedes build frontend work |
      | Project organization | One generated Diamond project per program, with build directories separated by target/backend | One project per program confirmed by user |
      | GUI persistence | HDL and authored constraints persist; manually transfer useful GUI project/strategy changes into build configuration | Manual transfer confirmed by user |
      | Initial migration | Preserve existing per-program HDL and LPFs; extract shared logic later | Proposed |
      | Initial validation programs | `tx30`, `rx30`, and `tx26_w_enable`, covering output, input, and enable-controlled routing | Confirmed by user |
      | Deliverables | Both `.jed` and `.bit`, reports, logs, provenance | Carried from earlier discussion |
      | Programming hardware | Separate future command; building never flashes a device | Proposed |
      | Netlist PDF and SVG exports | Add automated exports as later work, outside the first version | Confirmed by user |
      
      S2C, S3C, and older ispMACH compilation are outside the first implementation.
      Keep program, board target, and backend separate so they can be added without
      changing the command model. Do not promise that changing a target flag makes
      XO2-specific HDL portable to ispMACH.
      
      ## Documentation and repository findings
      
      UltraZohm uses a CPLD on each of D1–D5 for routing and voltage translation;
      programs may also implement safety logic. Rev05+ D-slot devices are distinct
      from the larger S3C device. See the [CPLD overview](https://ultrazohm.org/guide/CPLD/cpld.html).
      
      The documented authoring flow duplicates an implementation in
      `uz_d_slots.ldf`, edits VHDL and constraints in Diamond, and exports JEDEC.
      The proposed tooling automates that project work. See
      [creating a Diamond program](https://ultrazohm.org/guide/CPLD/diamond_create_program.html).
      Building and device programming are separate operations; the latter has a
      five-device D-slot chain and carrier-specific connection settings. See
      [programming documentation](https://ultrazohm.org/guide/CPLD/cpld_programming.html).
      
      Repository inspection:
      
      - `MACHXO2/` contains D-slot, S2C, and S3C projects. `ispMACH/` holds older
        device flows. There is no existing root Makefile or Python build frontend.
      - The D-slot root is
        `MACHXO2/D_Slot_CPLD_LCMXO2-2000HC-4TG100C/uz_d_slots/`.
        Its LDF declares nine LSE implementations, generally with top `SignalRouter`.
      - Its default implementation, `uz_d_abs_encoder_ssi_rev01`, references two
        missing files: its VHDL and LPF. The existing `uz_d_abs_encoder` directory
        must not be silently assumed to be that missing revision.
      - Nine source directories are outside that LDF: `i2c`, `tx16_14rx`,
        `tx20_10rx`, `uz_d_abs_encoder`, `uz_d_resolver_d4_4inverter`,
        `uz_d_resolver_d5_4inverter`, `uz_d_temperature_ltc2983`,
        `uz_d_voltage_003_5V_tx30`, and `uz_d_voltage_013_tx30`.
        Folder existence alone does not establish release readiness.
      - Program-local source LPFs form ten distinct groups after normalizing
        newlines. They contain I/O voltage, pull mode, placement, and configuration
        preferences. A single shared LPF cannot be substituted without reviewing
        those differences. For example, the `tx30` LPF assigns LVCMOS18 to FPGA-side
        signals and LVCMOS33 to adapter-side signals.
      - HDL repeats routing and safety code. In `tx30`, forwarding is gated by
        `reqsafestate`; `slotok` and `reqoe` are explicitly driven. The template uses
        an enable pattern on FPGA pins 26–29. Preserve these semantics during build
        migration; sharing code is a separate functional change.
      - The I2C area contains EFB IP and additional dependencies. It needs a complete
        source/library/IP inventory before joining the standard build set.
      - Source files coexist with exported `.jed`/`.bit`, generated LPFs, archives,
        and duplicate top-level VHDL files. Manifests must list exact inputs, never
        recursively glob all VHDL: many programs use the same entity name.
      - The LDF references `uz_d_slots1.sty`, which exists locally but is untracked.
        Capture the required strategy explicitly before claiming clean-checkout
        reproducibility. Existing binaries cannot establish their source provenance.
      - `xo2_libraries/` is also untracked and contains VHDL libraries. It is not
        referenced by the inspected D-slot LDF; adding it is not automatically
        necessary for the first routing builds.
      - No `diamond`, `pnmainc`, `yosys`, or `ghdl` executable was found on PATH.
        Podman is available. This is an environment observation, not proof that no
        vendor installation exists elsewhere. No synthesis has been run.
      
      `new_approach/design.md` proposes generated projects, optional open-source
      builds, GUI compatibility, and netlist exports. The accompanying
      `new_approach/toolchain.md` records the narrower Diamond-first choice and a
      headless container requirement. This plan carries that direction forward.
      
      ## Architecture and interface
      
      Use Make for convenient commands; put validation, path handling, scaffolding,
      artifact collection, and backend dispatch in Python. The Python CLI should
      also work directly, particularly if Windows support is selected. Prefer
      the container's Python 3.10 with `tomli`, with a standard-library `tomllib`
      fallback path on Python 3.11+. Ubuntu 22.04 was selected for Diamond runtime
      compatibility.
      
      ```text
      Makefile
      buildsystem/                 Python CLI and Diamond Tcl generation
      programs/<name>/             program.toml and editable VHDL
      targets/rev05_dslot/         target.toml and reviewed board constraints
      common/                     shared HDL only when deliberately extracted
      templates/                  named program templates
      containers/diamond/         pinned environment recipe
      build/<program>/<target>/<backend>/
          project/                generated LDF, strategy, Tcl, tool intermediates
          artifacts/              firmware.jed, firmware.bit, reports, build.json
      ```
      
      During migration, manifests may reference the existing source directories;
      moving every legacy file is not a prerequisite. Keep the existing projects
      and released binaries available while validating the new flow.
      
      ```sh
      make list
      make doctor
      make new NAME=my_adapter TEMPLATE=tx30 TARGET=rev05_dslot
      make check PROGRAM=my_adapter
      make project PROGRAM=my_adapter
      make build PROGRAM=my_adapter TARGET=rev05_dslot
      make gui PROGRAM=my_adapter TARGET=rev05_dslot
      make build-all TARGET=rev05_dslot
      make clean PROGRAM=my_adapter TARGET=rev05_dslot
      ```
      
      `build` is the default target. `TARGET` defaults to `rev05_dslot`; backend
      defaults come from target metadata. A later `TOOLCHAIN=...` override selects
      only an implemented, compatible backend. `build-all` uses an explicit catalog
      of supported programs and reports failures; it excludes templates and archives.
      `new` must refuse an existing destination and create all required authored
      files without opening Diamond. `clean` removes only the selected generated
      build directory.
      
      Program manifests record name, top entity, ordered source list with VHDL
      libraries, language standard, supported targets, constraint files, and any
      required capabilities. Target manifests record board identity, exact device,
      default backend, and configuration/strategy baseline. Backend-specific options
      belong in an explicit Diamond section; do not invent universal translations
      for options that another backend may not support.
      
      Start with exact per-program LPFs. Later, factor reviewed common board
      placements from adapter-specific electrical/timing preferences. Reject
      conflicting assignments rather than relying on accidental file precedence.
      Keep D-slot position separate from target identity: a resolver's D5 mapping is
      a program variant, while device-chain position belongs to programming setup.
      
      ## Headless and GUI contract
      
      Diamond supports Tcl-driven project processing from the command line. The
      [Lattice Diamond user guide](https://www.latticesemi.com/-/media/LatticeSemi/Documents/UserManuals/JL/LatticeDiamondUserGuide.ashx?document_id=41988)
      documents project opening and synthesis, translation, map, PAR, and export
      commands. Confirm the launcher and JEDEC/bitstream export tasks against the
      selected installed version; do not assume an old Windows command example is
      the correct Linux invocation.
      
      The backend prepares the project through Diamond Tcl, runs the vendor command
      line tools, and collects outputs. Pin the Diamond version and LSE strategy.
      Require both fresh exports before marking a build successful. Propagate errors
      and preserve logs; a stale programming file must never mask a failed build.
      
      The generated GUI project references authored HDL and LPFs in the checkout.
      Opening and saving those files in Diamond therefore changes the real inputs.
      Generated strategy/project metadata remains disposable. Useful GUI changes to
      source membership or strategy must be recorded in manifests/backend settings.
      Document this explicitly, and detect modified generated configuration before
      regeneration so experiments are not silently lost. Manual transfer is the
      confirmed initial workflow; automatic GUI settings import is deferred.
      
      When constraint composition is introduced, distinguish authored LPFs from the
      generated effective LPF. Editing a generated effective LPF cannot count as a
      persistent source change. Validate the actual Spreadsheet View save behavior
      in the selected Diamond version before promising direct GUI constraint edits.
      
      Use relative source references where Diamond supports them. Container and host
      GUI project preparation must share settings but may regenerate host-specific
      paths. Verify reopening from another checkout location. A build and GUI session
      must not write the same implementation directory concurrently; use a lock.
      
      Provide a pinned Linux container recipe using a locally supplied installer.
      Configure the license at runtime, keep it outside the image/repository, and
      verify the license arrangement with the actual installation. Native and
      container builds use the same backend scripts. Acceptance requires a build
      with no display server, no GUI interaction, and no interactive terminal.
      Native GUI operation is tested separately; no container desktop is required.
      
      ## Artifacts and verification
      
      Each successful build produces `.jed`, `.bit`, vendor reports and logs, and
      `build.json` with source/configuration hashes, Git revision and dirty status,
      tool version, selected target/backend/options, and output hashes. Ignore new
      scratch output under `build/`; decide separately how release binaries are
      published. Preserve the repository's existing versioned deliverables.
      
      Verify manifest errors, missing sources, duplicate names, unsupported targets,
      scaffold overwrite handling, path quoting, and failure/stale-output handling.
      Run actual Diamond smoke builds for `tx30`, `rx30`, then `tx26_w_enable`.
      Review pin/I/O reports and combinational path delays;
      clocked programs additionally need explicit clock constraints and timing checks.
      An unconstrained design must not be described as having passed timing closure.
      
      Compare legacy and generated-project builds using the same source files,
      constraints, and tool settings. Compare configuration payloads where practical,
      plus pin and utilization reports; file headers/timestamps can prevent bytewise
      identity. Add functional checks for routing, enable patterns and safe-state
      behavior before refactoring HDL. Hardware validation is a distinct release
      milestone, not implied by successful synthesis.
      
      The open-source backend remains an extension: upstream
      [nextpnr](https://github.com/YosysHQ/nextpnr) labels MachXO2 support experimental,
      and VHDL needs a suitable frontend such as
      [GHDL/Yosys](https://github.com/ghdl/ghdl-yosys-plugin).
      The exact XO2 packing/export commands and artifact formats in the earlier
      discussion have not been validated here. Do not promise `.jed` generation or
      equivalence to Diamond until demonstrated on this target.
      
      Likewise, automated Diamond Netlist Analyzer PDF export is not an established
      requirement or proven CLI capability. A later GHDL/Yosys/Graphviz analysis path
      can provide independent schematics, clearly labeled with the producing tool
      and synthesis stage rather than presented as Diamond's implemented netlist.

      Is it feasable to use a fully open source toolchain for lattice xo2-2000?
      
      Yes. For the Lattice MachXO2-2000, a genuinely end-to-end open-source flow is feasible today, including programming the internal flash:
      
      Verilog/SystemVerilog → Yosys → nextpnr-machxo2 → Project Trellis → openFPGALoader
      
      The important caveat is that MachXO2 support in nextpnr is still officially labelled experimental, so I would distinguish between “feasible and useful” and “drop-in replacement for Diamond for every design.”
      
      For the LCMXO2-2000 specifically, Project Trellis has explicit device support. Its database contains the LCMXO2-2000HC, including TQFP100, CSBGA132, TQFP144, CABGA256 and FTBGA256 packages, as well as HE and ZE variants. That means the LCMXO2-2000HC you're using on the newer UltraZohm hardware is not an unsupported edge case.
      
      A contemporary flow looks approximately like:
      
                    HDL
                     │
                     ▼
              ┌─────────────┐
              │    Yosys    │
              │synth_lattice│
              │ -family xo2 │
              └──────┬──────┘
                     │ JSON
                     ▼
            ┌──────────────────┐
            │ nextpnr-machxo2  │
            │ place + route    │
            └────────┬─────────┘
                     │ configuration
                     ▼
              ┌─────────────┐
              │ prjtrellis  │
              │  ecppack    │
              └──────┬──────┘
                     │ .bit/.jed
                     ▼
           ┌───────────────────┐
           │ openFPGALoader    │
           │       JTAG        │
           └─────────┬─────────┘
                     ▼
               LCMXO2-2000
      
      Modern Yosys uses:
      
      yosys -p "
          read_verilog top.v;
          synth_lattice -family xo2 -top top -json top.json
      "
      
      Older examples say synth_machxo2; that pass was replaced by synth_lattice -family xo2.
      
      Then the architecture backend is nextpnr-machxo2. It's a real upstream nextpnr backend, not some abandoned third-party fork. Building it is explicitly documented by nextpnr:
      
      cmake .. \
          -DARCH=machxo2 \
          -DTRELLIS_INSTALL_PREFIX=/usr/local
      
      make -j$(nproc)
      
      Project Trellis provides the reverse-engineered device database and configuration/bitstream tooling. The database specifically documents the LCMXO2-2000 architecture.
      
      And importantly, programming doesn't require Diamond Programmer either. openFPGALoader explicitly supports MachXO2 2000, both SRAM and internal flash. It can program MachXO2 .jed/.bit images through supported JTAG adapters.
      
      Where I would be cautious
      
      The main issue isn't basic LUTs, FFs, counters, state machines, UARTs, GPIO etc. Those are exactly the sort of designs I'd be comfortable trying immediately.
      
      The bigger risk is special MachXO2 functionality:
      
      PLLs / clock routing
      EBR/block RAM corner cases
      unusual I/O modes
      DDR primitives
      Embedded Function Block
      UFM
      unusual global clock arrangements
      precise timing closure
      
      The nextpnr project itself continues to describe MachXO2 as experimental, and there have been recent open issues around MachXO2 device/backend handling. So for a CPLD-style control application I'd expect a much easier experience than for a design trying to exercise every MachXO2 primitive.
      
      For your UltraZohm CPLD use case, this distinction matters. If the XO2-2000 design is primarily interlocks, combinational logic, state machines, PWM/gate routing, fault handling and ordinary clocked logic, I think switching to an open-source flow is quite realistic. If it heavily uses Lattice-generated IP, I'd first inventory those primitives.
      
      I would not remove Diamond immediately
      
      I'd initially make the build reproducible using both:
      
                        ┌─ Diamond ───────► reference bitstream
      RTL + constraints ┤
                        └─ Yosys/nextpnr ─► open bitstream
      
      Then run the same functional tests on both.
      
      Once your particular XO2 application passes hardware regression tests, you can make the open flow the primary CI build. The nice benefit is that Yosys + nextpnr are vastly easier to put into a headless Linux container/CI environment than Diamond, with no FlexNet licensing involved.
      
      There is even an existing upstream nextpnr MachXO2 test flow doing post-P&R simulation/equivalence checking, so the infrastructure for fairly rigorous validation exists.
      
      So my assessment: yes, I would seriously try it for the XO2-2000 rather than spending more effort fighting Diamond/FlexNet. The one qualification is that I'd validate your actual CPLD design against the Diamond-generated version before making it the only production flow.
      
      I can also put together a minimal Ubuntu/Docker XO2-2000HC project with Yosys + nextpnr + Trellis + openFPGALoader, including an LPF pin file and a one-command make flash flow.
      
      Yes. I would design it explicitly so the headless workflow does not prevent using Diamond GUI.
      
      The best model is:
      
      Repository files                    Generated Diamond project
      ----------------                    -------------------------
      program.vhd  ─────────────────────► project.ldf
      helper.vhd   ─────────────────────► implementation
      pins.lpf     ─────────────────────► Diamond metadata
      target.toml  ── build generator ──► ...
      
      Crucially, Diamond should reference the real VHDL and LPF files in the repository, rather than copying them into build/.
      
      Then you could have:
      
      make PROGRAM=inverter TARGET=rev05_dslot
      
      for the normal headless build, and:
      
      make gui PROGRAM=inverter TARGET=rev05_dslot
      
      which would:
      
      Generate the same Diamond project.
      Leave it somewhere predictable, e.g.
      build/inverter/rev05_dslot/diamond/project.ldf
      Launch:
      diamond build/inverter/rev05_dslot/diamond/project.ldf
      
      So you get the normal Diamond GUI with:
      
      VHDL hierarchy
      synthesis
      map/PAR
      reports
      timing analysis
      pin assignment
      implementation inspection
      Programmer integration, if desired
      
      while still having exactly the same project that CI builds.
      
      What GUI edits would persist?
      
      This is the important distinction.
      
      Edits to these should persist normally because they're real source files:
      
      programs/inverter/inverter.vhd
      common/foo.vhd
      targets/rev05_dslot/top.vhd
      targets/rev05_dslot/pins.lpf
      
      For example, if you double-click:
      
      inverter.vhd
      
      inside Diamond and edit it, you are editing the actual Git-controlled file.
      
      Similarly, ideally the LPF shown by Diamond is:
      
      targets/rev05_dslot/pins.lpf
      
      rather than:
      
      build/.../copied_pins.lpf
      
      So pin/constraint changes can also be retained.
      
      Diamond project settings are different
      
      Suppose you use the GUI to change:
      
      Synthesis strategy
      Optimization goal
      PAR effort
      Frequency constraints
      Implementation settings
      
      and Diamond writes those changes into:
      
      project.ldf
      
      That .ldf is generated, so the next:
      
      make clean
      make ...
      
      would erase those settings.
      
      I actually think that's desirable.
      
      It makes this distinction explicit:
      
      VHDL / LPF / target config
              │
              └── source of truth
      
      Diamond .ldf / implementation files
              │
              └── disposable representation
      
      If a GUI experiment turns out to be useful, you transfer that option into target.toml.
      
      For example:
      
      [synthesis]
      optimization = "speed"
      
      [par]
      effort = "high"
      
      The Diamond backend translates that to the corresponding Diamond option when generating the project.
      
      I would add three commands
      
      Something like:
      
      # Fully headless, intended for CI
      make build PROGRAM=foo TARGET=rev05_dslot
      
      # Generate project but don't build
      make project PROGRAM=foo TARGET=rev05_dslot
      
      # Generate project and open Diamond
      make gui PROGRAM=foo TARGET=rev05_dslot
      
      So:
      
                        program + target
                               │
                          build.py
                               │
                    generate Diamond project
                               │
                    ┌──────────┴──────────┐
                    │                     │
                 make build            make gui
                    │                     │
                pnmainc                 Diamond
                    │                     │
                headless             interactive
      
      Both workflows operate on the exact same generated project.
      
      This is actually better than keeping .ldf files in Git
      
      You still retain everything nice about Diamond for interactive development, but don't have the usual problem where:
      
      foo.ldf
      foo1.ldf
      foo_test.ldf
      foo_new.ldf
      impl1/
      impl2/
      strategy1.sty
      
      gradually become part of the repository.
      
      Instead, the GUI becomes another frontend to the same reproducible project definition.
      
      For UltraZohm I think this is the ideal compromise: headless/reproducible by default, Diamond GUI available whenever useful, and no vendor-project metadata as source of truth.
      
      Is it also possible to export the netlist analyzer pdf for diamand and/or the FOSS toolchain?
      
      Yes. I would make netlist schematics a first-class build artifact, but treat Diamond and the FOSS flow a little differently.
      
      For Diamond, the Netlist Analyzer can definitely export its schematic as PDF or SVG. Lattice documents File → Export; PDF exports the complete schematic as a multi-page document, whereas SVG exports the currently displayed sheet.
      
      The catch is automation: I cannot find a documented Diamond Tcl/pnmainc command equivalent to Vivado's write_schematic. The Diamond documentation describes Netlist Analyzer export as a GUI operation, while LSE itself can be run headlessly. So I would not make automated Diamond-PDF export a required part of CI unless we find an undocumented callable interface.
      
      For the FOSS side, this is actually much better. Yosys has the show command specifically for generating netlist schematics via Graphviz, and it can operate on arbitrary selections/modules and at arbitrary points in the synthesis flow.
      
      So we could have:
      
      make netlist PROGRAM=foo TARGET=rev05_dslot
      
      produce something like:
      
      build/foo/rev05_dslot/artifacts/
      ├── firmware.jed
      ├── firmware.bit
      ├── reports/
      │   ├── utilization.txt
      │   └── timing.txt
      └── netlist/
          ├── rtl.pdf
          ├── synthesized.pdf
          └── synthesized.svg
      
      For example, with Yosys:
      
      read VHDL
         ↓
      hierarchy/elaboration
         ↓
      show
         ↓
      rtl.dot
         ↓
      Graphviz
         ↓
      rtl.pdf
      
      and later:
      
      VHDL
       ↓
      Yosys synthesis
       ↓
      MachXO2 technology mapping
       ↓
      show
       ↓
      machxo2_synth.dot
       ↓
      Graphviz
       ↓
      synthesized.pdf
      
      Yosys explicitly supports writing a DOT file instead of launching the viewer, and Graphviz then handles the PDF generation.
      
      Something as simple as:
      
      yosys -p '
          ...
          show -format dot -prefix build/netlist/rtl top
      '
      
      dot -Tpdf \
          build/netlist/rtl.dot \
          -o build/netlist/rtl.pdf
      
      would be completely headless.
      
      Even with Diamond as the real compiler

      # Simulation and CI
      
      Implemented toolchain: **GHDL 4.1.0 + cocotb 2.0.0 + pytest + GTKWave**.
      The initial suite tests the actual manifest sources for `tx30`, `rx30`, and
      `tx26_w_enable`, using walking patterns, exhaustive enable/safe-state cases,
      and reproducible randomized transitions.
      
      With the simulation dependencies installed:
      
      ```sh
      make sim
      make sim PROGRAM=tx26_w_enable SEED=42
      gtkwave build/simulation/tx26_w_enable/waves.ghw
      ```
      
      Alternatively, use the Linux amd64 container:
      
      ```sh
      make sim-image
      make sim-container
      ```
      
      Each run produces waveforms, test results, logs, and source/seed provenance in
      `build/simulation/`. GitHub Actions runs the same container and retains these
      artifacts even if tests fail. `make test` runs the existing build frontend tests.
      
      See [the simulation guide](new_approach/docs/simulation.rst) for installation,
      FST output, behavior contracts, and adding more programs. The image pins the
      simulator archive and Python dependencies; OS packages can receive updates.
      
      Future work includes behavioral models for device-specific oscillator/EFB
      primitives and host-compiled UltraZohm C-driver integration through a cocotb
      bus bridge. Keep Ceedling for software unit tests. Drivers that access FPGA
      IP through AXI require that IP or an explicit model in the integration test.
      These extensions and full processor emulation are not part of the initial suite.

      # Toolchain Discussion
      
      ## User
      
      Is it feasable to use a fully open source toolchain for lattice xo2-2000?
      
      ## Assistant
      
      Yes. For the **Lattice MachXO2-2000**, a genuinely end-to-end open-source flow is feasible today, including programming the internal flash:
      
      **Verilog/SystemVerilog → Yosys → nextpnr-machxo2 → Project Trellis → openFPGALoader**
      
      The important caveat is that **MachXO2 support in nextpnr is still officially labelled experimental**, so I would distinguish between “feasible and useful” and “drop-in replacement for Diamond for every design.”
      
      For the **LCMXO2-2000 specifically**, Project Trellis has explicit device support. Its database contains the `LCMXO2-2000HC`, including TQFP100, CSBGA132, TQFP144, CABGA256 and FTBGA256 packages, as well as HE and ZE variants. That means the LCMXO2-2000HC you're using on the newer UltraZohm hardware is not an unsupported edge case.
      
      A contemporary flow looks approximately like:
      
      ```text
                    HDL
                     │
                     ▼
              ┌─────────────┐
              │    Yosys    │
              │synth_lattice│
              │ -family xo2 │
              └──────┬──────┘
                     │ JSON
                     ▼
            ┌──────────────────┐
            │ nextpnr-machxo2  │
            │ place + route    │
            └────────┬─────────┘
                     │ configuration
                     ▼
              ┌─────────────┐
              │ prjtrellis  │
              │  ecppack    │
              └──────┬──────┘
                     │ .bit/.jed
                     ▼
           ┌───────────────────┐
           │ openFPGALoader    │
           │       JTAG        │
           └─────────┬─────────┘
                     ▼
               LCMXO2-2000
      ```
      
      Modern Yosys uses:
      
      ```bash
      yosys -p "
          read_verilog top.v;
          synth_lattice -family xo2 -top top -json top.json
      "
      ```
      
      Older examples say `synth_machxo2`; that pass was replaced by `synth_lattice -family xo2`.
      
      Then the architecture backend is `nextpnr-machxo2`. It's a real upstream nextpnr backend, not some abandoned third-party fork. Building it is explicitly documented by nextpnr:
      
      ```bash
      cmake ..     -DARCH=machxo2     -DTRELLIS_INSTALL_PREFIX=/usr/local
      
      make -j$(nproc)
      ```
      
      Project Trellis provides the reverse-engineered device database and configuration/bitstream tooling. The database specifically documents the `LCMXO2-2000` architecture.
      
      And importantly, **programming doesn't require Diamond Programmer either**. `openFPGALoader` explicitly supports MachXO2 **2000**, both SRAM and internal flash. It can program MachXO2 `.jed`/`.bit` images through supported JTAG adapters.
      
      ### Where I would be cautious
      
      The main issue isn't basic LUTs, FFs, counters, state machines, UARTs, GPIO etc. Those are exactly the sort of designs I'd be comfortable trying immediately.
      
      The bigger risk is **special MachXO2 functionality**:
      
      - PLLs / clock routing
      - EBR/block RAM corner cases
      - unusual I/O modes
      - DDR primitives
      - Embedded Function Block
      - UFM
      - unusual global clock arrangements
      - precise timing closure
      
      The nextpnr project itself continues to describe MachXO2 as experimental, and there have been recent open issues around MachXO2 device/backend handling. So for a CPLD-style control application I'd expect a much easier experience than for a design trying to exercise every MachXO2 primitive.
      
      For **your UltraZohm CPLD use case**, this distinction matters. If the XO2-2000 design is primarily interlocks, combinational logic, state machines, PWM/gate routing, fault handling and ordinary clocked logic, I think switching to an open-source flow is **quite realistic**. If it heavily uses Lattice-generated IP, I'd first inventory those primitives.
      
      ### I would not remove Diamond immediately
      
      I'd initially make the build reproducible using both:
      
      ```text
                        ┌─ Diamond ───────► reference bitstream
      RTL + constraints ┤
                        └─ Yosys/nextpnr ─► open bitstream
      ```
      
      Then run the same functional tests on both.
      
      Once your particular XO2 application passes hardware regression tests, you can make the open flow the primary CI build. The nice benefit is that **Yosys + nextpnr are vastly easier to put into a headless Linux container/CI environment than Diamond**, with no FlexNet licensing involved.
      
      There is even an existing upstream nextpnr MachXO2 test flow doing post-P&R simulation/equivalence checking, so the infrastructure for fairly rigorous validation exists.
      
      **So my assessment:** yes, I would seriously try it for the XO2-2000 rather than spending more effort fighting Diamond/FlexNet. The one qualification is that I'd validate your actual CPLD design against the Diamond-generated version before making it the only production flow.
      
      I can also put together a minimal **Ubuntu/Docker XO2-2000HC project with Yosys + nextpnr + Trellis + openFPGALoader**, including an LPF pin file and a one-command `make flash` flow.

      ## User
      
      what about the older ispMACH `LA4128V`, any foss toolchain there?
      
      ## Assistant
      
      For the older **LA4128V / ispMACH 4000V** generation, the situation is much less complete than for MachXO2.
      
      There is now meaningful open-source work around the ispMACH 4000 architecture, but I would not currently call it a normal “Verilog → bitstream → program” FOSS toolchain.
      
      The interesting pieces are:
      
      - **`re4k`**: reverse-engineered fuse maps for ispMACH 4000 devices. It explicitly supports the **LC4128V** family in TQFP100/128/144.
      - **`Zig-LC4k`**: uses those fuse maps to construct configurations and generate **JEDEC or SVF** programming files. It supports LC4032/4064/4128 variants and can also disassemble existing JEDEC files.
      - An SVF can in principle then be executed with an open-source JTAG tool such as OpenOCD, so the actual programming side does not fundamentally require ispVM/Diamond.
      
      The big missing piece is the **fitter**:
      
      ```text
      Verilog / VHDL
            │
            ▼
          Yosys              possible synthesis
            │
            ▼
       logical equations
            │
            X   <-- no mature open-source ispMACH4000 fitter
            │
            ▼
      GLB / macrocell / PT placement
            │
            ▼
       fuse map
            │
            ▼
       JEDEC / SVF
      ```
      
      `Zig-LC4k` deliberately does **not** synthesize Verilog/VHDL/ABEL. Instead, you manually describe macrocells, product terms, routing, clocks, etc. in Zig.
      
      So today you essentially have three options.
      
      ### 1. Fully FOSS, but manually mapped
      
      For relatively simple CPLD logic:
      
      ```text
      Zig-LC4k logic expressions
              ↓
      manual macrocell/GLB assignment
              ↓
      Zig-LC4k
              ↓
      .jed / .svf
              ↓
      OpenOCD / other SVF player
              ↓
      ispMACH 4000
      ```
      
      This really can be fully open source, but you still have to deal with placement/routing yourself.
      
      ### 2. FOSS synthesis + proprietary fitter
      
      A more practical transitional solution would be something like:
      
      ```text
      Verilog
        ↓
      Yosys
        ↓
      EDIF / equations
        ↓
      lpf4k.exe
        ↓
      JEDEC
      ```
      
      `lpf4k` is the old Lattice ispMACH4000 fitter. It is the critical proprietary component that does the macrocell/product-term allocation.
      
      ### 3. Write an open-source fitter
      
      The hard reverse-engineering work appears to have been done already by `re4k`. The project documents routing, product terms, macrocells, clocks, set/reset, OE, I/O configuration and output routing.
      
      So an open-source fitter would essentially need to solve:
      
      ```text
      Yosys netlist
         ↓
      Boolean/product-term decomposition
         ↓
      choose GLB
         ↓
      choose macrocell
         ↓
      allocate product terms
         ↓
      allocate GRP signals
         ↓
      allocate cluster routing
         ↓
      configure I/O
         ↓
      Zig-LC4k / re4k fuse writer
      ```
      
      ### The complication for your exact LA4128V
      
      Your device is **LA4128V**, not LC4128V.
      
      The `LA` versions are the automotive-qualified ispMACH 4000 parts. `re4k` notes that automotive LA4xxx variants likely use the same fusemaps as their LC counterparts, but that this is conjecture.
      
      So:
      
      **LC4128V: reverse engineered and supported.
      LA4128V: very probably architecturally identical, but not verified by the project.**
      
      There is an additional issue for UltraZohm: **LC4256V isn't supported by re4k/Zig-LC4k yet**.
      
      So an open flow aimed at all older UltraZohm revisions would currently have to solve both:
      
      ```text
      LA4128V
          └── verify whether LC4128V fuse map is identical
      
      LC4256V
          └── reverse-engineer/add device support
      ```
      
      ### What I would do for UltraZohm
      
      A reasonable migration path is:
      
      ```text
      Rev05+
      MachXO2-2000/4000
          ↓
      Yosys + nextpnr + Trellis
          ↓
      fully FOSS
      ```
      
      while initially leaving
      
      ```text
      Rev01–Rev04
      LA4128V / LC4256V
          ↓
      ispLEVER Classic
      ```
      
      alone.

      ## User
      
      Lets forget the FOSS pipeline for the moment and foucs on just headless builds. Read the CPLD documentation for the ultrazohm at https://ultrazohm.org/guide/CPLD/cpld.html. What I really want is a headless and script based method to build all the bitstreams + .jed files. This means I need diamond and isplever in a headless container. I then want scripts / makefiels that build the bitstreams and scripts that create new projects based on templates to remove all the manual project overhead. Effectively, there are only .vhdl files.       ## Assistant
      
      After reading the current CPLD documentation, I think the cleanest solution is to **stop treating Diamond/ispLEVER projects as source code at all**.
      
      The source of truth should become:
      
      ```text
      VHDL program
      + target description
      + target-specific pin constraints
      + build scripts
      ```
      
      and `.ldf`, `.syn`, temporary synthesis files, reports, etc. should be generated into `build/`.
      
      The developer workflow should become something like:
      
      ```bash
      make PROGRAM=optical_30tx TARGET=la4128v
      make PROGRAM=optical_30tx TARGET=lc4256v
      make PROGRAM=optical_30tx TARGET=xo2-2000
      make PROGRAM=optical_30tx all-targets
      make new NAME=my_new_adapter
      ```
      
      with generated output under:
      
      ```text
      build/
      └── optical_30tx/
          ├── la4128v/
          ├── lc4256v/
          └── xo2-2000/
      ```
      
      The repository should separate common logic, programs and target wrappers/constraints:
      
      ```text
      src/
      ├── common/
      ├── programs/
      └── targets/
          ├── la4128v/
          ├── lc4256v/
          ├── xo2-2000/
          └── xo2-4000-s3c/
      ```
      
      A common logical core plus small target wrappers is preferable to one monolithic conditional top-level because Rev05 has genuinely different safety/S3C functionality and MachXO2 has more capabilities than the older ispMACH devices.
      
      Target metadata could be machine-readable, for example:
      
      ```toml
      name = "xo2-2000"
      toolchain = "diamond"
      
      device = "LCMXO2-2000HC-4TG100C"
      top = "uz_dslot_xo2"
      constraints = "pins.lpf"
      
      has_s3c_interface = true
      has_internal_oscillator = true
      ```
      
      Diamond is the easier half because it supports Tcl project creation and headless execution. A generated script can create the project, add VHDL/LPF files and run synthesis, translate, map, PAR, bitstream generation and JEDEC generation via `pnmainc`.
      
      Conceptually:
      
      ```text
      make
       ↓
      generate build.tcl
       ↓
      pnmainc build.tcl
       ↓
      .jed + .bit + reports
      ```
      
      No `.ldf` needs to exist in Git.
      
      For ispLEVER, the main uncertainty is the headless/containerized execution path. The ultimate goal should be to capture the command-line synthesis/fitter flow and hide it behind the same build interface.
      
      Licensing should ideally be external to disposable build containers, using a stable license host/server where appropriate.
      
      The repository should keep only source and configuration, not generated vendor metadata such as `.ldf`, `.syn`, implementation directories or intermediate netlists.

      A possible repository layout:
      
      ```text
      cpld/
      ├── Makefile
      ├── programs/
      ├── targets/
      │   ├── rev05_dslot/
      │   └── rev05_s3c/
      ├── common/
      ├── buildsystem/
      │   ├── build.py
      │   ├── model.py
      ```

      The important rule is that `programs/`, `targets/` and `common/` remain toolchain-independent.
      
      A normalized target description might contain:
      
      ```toml
      name = "rev05_dslot"
      
      device = "LCMXO2-2000HC"
      package = "TQFP100"

      ```

      ```python
      class BuildBackend:
          def prepare(self, build):
              ...
      
          def build(self, build):
              ...
      
          def collect_artifacts(self, build):
              ...
      ```
      
      Diamond would generate its project entirely in `build/`, execute the generated Tcl with `pnmainc`, and then collect standardized artifacts such as:
      
      ```text
      artifacts/
      ├── firmware.jed
      ├── firmware.bit
      ├── timing.txt
      ├── utilization.txt
      └── build.json
      ```

      ```make
      PROGRAM ?=
      TARGET ?= rev05_dslot
      TOOLCHAIN ?=
      ```

      ```text
      ├── program.toml
      └── my_board.vhd
      ```

      The target should represent the **board**, e.g. `rev05_dslot`, not simply the FPGA type, because pinout and carrier behavior are board-revision properties.
      
      Toolchain and target should remain orthogonal:

      ```text
      target = rev05_dslot
      toolchain = diamond
      ```
      
      not:

      For now, only the Diamond backend needs implementation. The architecture merely reserves room for ispLEVER and FOSS backends later.

      ```text
                            VHDL
      ```

      Because the source is VHDL, the FOSS analysis path would likely use GHDL + Yosys.

      ```text
      netlist/
      ├── rtl/
      │   ├── top.pdf
      │   ├── program.pdf
      ```

      Verilog/SystemVerilog → Yosys → nextpnr-machxo2 → Project Trellis → openFPGALoader
      
      The important caveat is that MachXO2 support in nextpnr is still officially labelled experimental, so I would distinguish between “feasible and useful” and “drop-in replacement for Diamond for every design.”
      
      For the LCMXO2-2000 specifically, Project Trellis has explicit device support. Its database contains the LCMXO2-2000HC, including TQFP100, CSBGA132, TQFP144, CABGA256 and FTBGA256 packages, as well as HE and ZE variants. That means the LCMXO2-2000HC you're using on the newer UltraZohm hardware is not an unsupported edge case.
      
      A contemporary flow looks approximately like:
      
                    HDL
                     │
                     ▼
              ┌─────────────┐
              │    Yosys    │
              │synth_lattice│
              │ -family xo2 │
              └──────┬──────┘
                     │ JSON
                     ▼
            ┌──────────────────┐
            │ nextpnr-machxo2  │
            │ place + route    │
            └────────┬─────────┘
                     │ configuration
                     ▼
              ┌─────────────┐
              │ prjtrellis  │
              │  ecppack    │
              └──────┬──────┘
                     │ .bit/.jed
                     ▼
           ┌───────────────────┐
           │ openFPGALoader    │
           │       JTAG        │
           └─────────┬─────────┘
                     ▼
               LCMXO2-2000
      
      Modern Yosys uses:
      
      yosys -p "
          read_verilog top.v;
          synth_lattice -family xo2 -top top -json top.json
      "
      
      Older examples say synth_machxo2; that pass was replaced by synth_lattice -family xo2.
      
      Then the architecture backend is nextpnr-machxo2. It's a real upstream nextpnr backend, not some abandoned third-party fork. Building it is explicitly documented by nextpnr:
      
      cmake .. \
          -DARCH=machxo2 \
          -DTRELLIS_INSTALL_PREFIX=/usr/local
      
      make -j$(nproc)
      
      Project Trellis provides the reverse-engineered device database and configuration/bitstream tooling. The database specifically documents the LCMXO2-2000 architecture.
      
      And importantly, programming doesn't require Diamond Programmer either. openFPGALoader explicitly supports MachXO2 2000, both SRAM and internal flash. It can program MachXO2 .jed/.bit images through supported JTAG adapters.
      
      Where I would be cautious
      
      The main issue isn't basic LUTs, FFs, counters, state machines, UARTs, GPIO etc. Those are exactly the sort of designs I'd be comfortable trying immediately.
      
      The bigger risk is special MachXO2 functionality:
      
      PLLs / clock routing
      EBR/block RAM corner cases
      unusual I/O modes
      DDR primitives
      Embedded Function Block
      UFM
      unusual global clock arrangements
      precise timing closure
      
      The nextpnr project itself continues to describe MachXO2 as experimental, and there have been recent open issues around MachXO2 device/backend handling. So for a CPLD-style control application I'd expect a much easier experience than for a design trying to exercise every MachXO2 primitive.
      
      For your UltraZohm CPLD use case, this distinction matters. If the XO2-2000 design is primarily interlocks, combinational logic, state machines, PWM/gate routing, fault handling and ordinary clocked logic, I think switching to an open-source flow is quite realistic. If it heavily uses Lattice-generated IP, I'd first inventory those primitives.
      
      I would not remove Diamond immediately
      
      I'd initially make the build reproducible using both:
      
                        ┌─ Diamond ───────► reference bitstream
      RTL + constraints ┤
                        └─ Yosys/nextpnr ─► open bitstream
      
      Then run the same functional tests on both.
      
      Once your particular XO2 application passes hardware regression tests, you can make the open flow the primary CI build. The nice benefit is that Yosys + nextpnr are vastly easier to put into a headless Linux container/CI environment than Diamond, with no FlexNet licensing involved.
      
      There is even an existing upstream nextpnr MachXO2 test flow doing post-P&R simulation/equivalence checking, so the infrastructure for fairly rigorous validation exists.
      
      So my assessment: yes, I would seriously try it for the XO2-2000 rather than spending more effort fighting Diamond/FlexNet. The one qualification is that I'd validate your actual CPLD design against the Diamond-generated version before making it the only production flow.
      
      I can also put together a minimal Ubuntu/Docker XO2-2000HC project with Yosys + nextpnr + Trellis + openFPGALoader, including an LPF pin file and a one-command make flash flow.
      
      Yes. I would design it explicitly so the headless workflow does not prevent using Diamond GUI.
      
      The best model is:
      
      Repository files                    Generated Diamond project
      ----------------                    -------------------------
      program.vhd  ─────────────────────► project.ldf
      helper.vhd   ─────────────────────► implementation
      pins.lpf     ─────────────────────► Diamond metadata
      target.toml  ── build generator ──► ...
      
      Crucially, Diamond should reference the real VHDL and LPF files in the repository, rather than copying them into build/.
      
      Then you could have:
      
      make PROGRAM=inverter TARGET=rev05_dslot
      
      for the normal headless build, and:
      
      make gui PROGRAM=inverter TARGET=rev05_dslot
      
      which would:
      
      Generate the same Diamond project.
      Leave it somewhere predictable, e.g.
      build/inverter/rev05_dslot/diamond/project.ldf
      Launch:
      diamond build/inverter/rev05_dslot/diamond/project.ldf
      
      So you get the normal Diamond GUI with:
      
      VHDL hierarchy
      synthesis
      map/PAR
      reports
      timing analysis
      pin assignment
      implementation inspection
      Programmer integration, if desired
      
      while still having exactly the same project that CI builds.
      
      What GUI edits would persist?
      
      This is the important distinction.
      
      Edits to these should persist normally because they're real source files:
      
      programs/inverter/inverter.vhd
      common/foo.vhd
      targets/rev05_dslot/top.vhd
      targets/rev05_dslot/pins.lpf
      
      For example, if you double-click:
      
      inverter.vhd
      
      inside Diamond and edit it, you are editing the actual Git-controlled file.
      
      Similarly, ideally the LPF shown by Diamond is:
      
      targets/rev05_dslot/pins.lpf
      
      rather than:
      
      build/.../copied_pins.lpf
      
      So pin/constraint changes can also be retained.
      
      Diamond project settings are different
      
      Suppose you use the GUI to change:
      
      Synthesis strategy
      Optimization goal
      PAR effort
      Frequency constraints
      Implementation settings
      
      and Diamond writes those changes into:
      
      project.ldf
      
      That .ldf is generated, so the next:
      
      make clean
      make ...
      
      would erase those settings.
      
      I actually think that's desirable.
      
      It makes this distinction explicit:
      
      VHDL / LPF / target config
              │
              └── source of truth
      
      Diamond .ldf / implementation files
              │
              └── disposable representation
      
      If a GUI experiment turns out to be useful, you transfer that option into target.toml.
      
      For example:
      
      [synthesis]
      optimization = "speed"
      
      [par]
      effort = "high"
      
      The Diamond backend translates that to the corresponding Diamond option when generating the project.
      
      I would add three commands
      
      Something like:
      
      # Fully headless, intended for CI
      make build PROGRAM=foo TARGET=rev05_dslot
      
      # Generate project but don't build
      make project PROGRAM=foo TARGET=rev05_dslot
      
      # Generate project and open Diamond
      make gui PROGRAM=foo TARGET=rev05_dslot
      
      So:
      
                        program + target
                               │
                          build.py
                               │
                    generate Diamond project
                               │
                    ┌──────────┴──────────┐
                    │                     │
                 make build            make gui
                    │                     │
                pnmainc                 Diamond
                    │                     │
                headless             interactive
      
      Both workflows operate on the exact same generated project.
      
      This is actually better than keeping .ldf files in Git
      
      You still retain everything nice about Diamond for interactive development, but don't have the usual problem where:
      
      foo.ldf
      foo1.ldf
      foo_test.ldf
      foo_new.ldf
      impl1/
      impl2/
      strategy1.sty
      
      gradually become part of the repository.
      
      Instead, the GUI becomes another frontend to the same reproducible project definition.
      
      For UltraZohm I think this is the ideal compromise: headless/reproducible by default, Diamond GUI available whenever useful, and no vendor-project metadata as source of truth.
      
      Is it also possible to export the netlist analyzer pdf for diamand and/or the FOSS toolchain?
      
      Yes. I would make netlist schematics a first-class build artifact, but treat Diamond and the FOSS flow a little differently.
      
      For Diamond, the Netlist Analyzer can definitely export its schematic as PDF or SVG. Lattice documents File → Export; PDF exports the complete schematic as a multi-page document, whereas SVG exports the currently displayed sheet.
      
      The catch is automation: I cannot find a documented Diamond Tcl/pnmainc command equivalent to Vivado's write_schematic. The Diamond documentation describes Netlist Analyzer export as a GUI operation, while LSE itself can be run headlessly. So I would not make automated Diamond-PDF export a required part of CI unless we find an undocumented callable interface.
      
      For the FOSS side, this is actually much better. Yosys has the show command specifically for generating netlist schematics via Graphviz, and it can operate on arbitrary selections/modules and at arbitrary points in the synthesis flow.
      
      So we could have:
      
      make netlist PROGRAM=foo TARGET=rev05_dslot
      
      produce something like:
      
      build/foo/rev05_dslot/artifacts/
      ├── firmware.jed
      ├── firmware.bit
      ├── reports/
      │   ├── utilization.txt
      │   └── timing.txt
      └── netlist/
          ├── rtl.pdf
          ├── synthesized.pdf
          └── synthesized.svg
      
      For example, with Yosys:
      
      read VHDL
         ↓
      hierarchy/elaboration
         ↓
      show
         ↓
      rtl.dot
         ↓
      Graphviz
         ↓
      rtl.pdf
      
      and later:
      
      VHDL
       ↓
      Yosys synthesis
       ↓
      MachXO2 technology mapping
       ↓
      show
       ↓
      machxo2_synth.dot
       ↓
      Graphviz
       ↓
      synthesized.pdf
      
      Yosys explicitly supports writing a DOT file instead of launching the viewer, and Graphviz then handles the PDF generation.
      
      Something as simple as:
      
      yosys -p '
          ...
          show -format dot -prefix build/netlist/rtl top
      '
      
      dot -Tpdf \
          build/netlist/rtl.dot \
          -o build/netlist/rtl.pdf
      
      would be completely headless.
      
      Even with Diamond as the real compiler
      
      An interesting option is to use Diamond for the actual bitstream while using a FOSS synthesis/elaboration step only to create documentation:
      
                            VHDL
                             │
                   ┌─────────┴─────────┐
                   │                   │
                   ▼                   ▼
             Diamond / LSE       GHDL + Yosys
                   │                   │
            official build        schematic only
                   │                   │
              .jed / .bit           PDF / SVG
      
      That fits the backend-neutral architecture we discussed very nicely.
      
      We could define artifacts generically:
      
      backend output:
          bitstream
          jedec
          timing_report
          utilization_report
      
      analysis output:
          rtl_netlist_pdf
          synthesized_netlist_pdf
      
      The analysis step then doesn't even have to be tied to the implementation backend.
      
      There is one caveat: since your source is VHDL, a Yosys-based analysis path needs an appropriate VHDL frontend, typically GHDL integrated with Yosys. But that is perfectly reasonable for this use case.
      
      I'd generate more than one view
      
      A giant flattened CPLD schematic quickly becomes fairly useless. Instead I would generate:
      
      netlist/
      ├── rtl/
      │   ├── top.pdf
      │   ├── program.pdf
      │   └── safety_interface.pdf
      │
      └── synthesized/
          ├── top.pdf
          └── program.pdf
      
      Yosys lets us select individual modules or subsets of cells before show, so this can be deterministic and scriptable.
      
      Then:
      
      make docs PROGRAM=foo
      
      could automatically produce all of them.
      
      Diamond GUI remains useful too
      
      With the generated Diamond project approach:
      
      make gui PROGRAM=foo
      
      opens the same project in Diamond, and you can still do:
      
      Tools → Netlist Analyzer → File → Export → PDF
      
      when you specifically want Lattice's rendering. Diamond's Netlist Analyzer is designed around LSE's synthesized representation, so that PDF is useful as the vendor-tool view of what LSE produced.
      
      So I would support both:
      
      make netlist PROGRAM=foo
      
      → fully automated Yosys/GHDL PDF
      
      and:
      
      make gui PROGRAM=foo
      
      → Diamond Netlist Analyzer, with manual PDF export available.
      
      If we later discover a reliable undocumented Diamond CLI mechanism for schematic export, we can add it as an optional backend capability:
      
      DiamondBackend:
          build            ✓
          bitstream        ✓
          jedec            ✓
          netlist_gui      ✓
          netlist_pdf_cli  ?
      
      
      TrellisBackend:
          build            ✓
          bitstream        ✓
          netlist_pdf_cli  ✓

      ## Artifacts and verification
      
      Each successful build produces `.jed`, `.bit`, vendor reports and logs, and
      `build.json` with source/configuration hashes, Git revision and dirty status,
      tool version, selected target/backend/options, and output hashes. Ignore new
      scratch output under `build/`; decide separately how release binaries are
      published. Preserve the repository's existing versioned deliverables.
      
      Verify manifest errors, missing sources, duplicate names, unsupported targets,
      scaffold overwrite handling, path quoting, and failure/stale-output handling.
      Run actual Diamond smoke builds for `tx30`, `rx30`, then `tx26_w_enable`.
      Review pin/I/O reports and combinational path delays;
      clocked programs additionally need explicit clock constraints and timing checks.
      An unconstrained design must not be described as having passed timing closure.
      
      Compare legacy and generated-project builds using the same source files,
      constraints, and tool settings. Compare configuration payloads where practical,
      plus pin and utilization reports; file headers/timestamps can prevent bytewise
      identity. Add functional checks for routing, enable patterns and safe-state
      behavior before refactoring HDL. Hardware validation is a distinct release
      milestone, not implied by successful synthesis.
      
      The open-source backend remains an extension: upstream
      [nextpnr](https://github.com/YosysHQ/nextpnr) labels MachXO2 support experimental,
      and VHDL needs a suitable frontend such as
      [GHDL/Yosys](https://github.com/ghdl/ghdl-yosys-plugin).
      The exact XO2 packing/export commands and artifact formats in the earlier
      discussion have not been validated here. Do not promise `.jed` generation or
      equivalence to Diamond until demonstrated on this target.
      
      Likewise, automated Diamond Netlist Analyzer PDF export is not an established
      requirement or proven CLI capability. A later GHDL/Yosys/Graphviz analysis path
      can provide independent schematics, clearly labeled with the producing tool
      and synthesis stage rather than presented as Diamond's implemented netlist.

      separate checkout path with spaces and matched the `tx30` reference. The repeatable
